title: Optimal polynomial-time approximation ratio for metric k-means
area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
formal: Determine \(\rho_{\mathrm{MetKM}}\), the infimum of achievable expected approximation ratios for metric k-means with an explicit set of possible centers.
definitions: An instance consists of a finite labeled set U with its entire rational distance matrix \(d:U\times U\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\), nonempty subsets D,F of U with \(D\subseteq F\), and an integer \(1\le k\le|F|\). Require \(d(u,v)=0\) exactly when u=v, symmetry, and the triangle inequality. D is the unweighted client set and F the possible centers. A solution is a subset \(S\subseteq F\) of cardinality k, of cost \(\sum_{x\in D}\min_{s\in S}d(x,s)^2\). OPT is the minimum of this cost over all such S. The squared cost itself need not satisfy the triangle inequality. The metric is unrestricted and fully listed; neither a Euclidean promise nor a distance oracle is provided. An algorithm is a uniform randomized Turing machine with independent fair random bits. Its worst-case running time, over all random tapes, is polynomial in the binary input length. It always returns a feasible solution, and its expected cost is measured over its coins. A real number \(r\ge1\) is achievable if one such algorithm satisfies \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}(A(I))]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) for every valid instance I. The target is the infimum of achievable r; the polynomial and algorithm may depend on r. An infimum need not be attained. All integers and rational input data use explicit binary encodings, with numerator and positive denominator for each rational; their full lengths count toward the input size. No complexity assumption is built into the definition.

context_blocks.text: Metric k-means squares the underlying distances, unlike k-median. The admissible center set is explicit, and opening extra centers does not meet the card’s feasibility condition.

The July 2026 paper reports a ratio approaching 4.9 and discusses a much larger known hardness barrier for general metrics than for the Euclidean setting. A bound under a complexity assumption is not an unconditional determination of the algorithmic infimum.

why: Determine the computational limit of squared-distance clustering in arbitrary metrics, a central network and data-clustering approximation problem.

answer_criterion: Supply a real number a and a complete Lean-checked proof that its absolute difference from the defined constant is at most \(1/100\). A proved containing interval of width at most \(1/50\) qualifies through its midpoint. The constant is unconditional: a lower bound relying on an unproved complexity assumption settles only the corresponding conditional statement. Merely restating the defining infimum is not a determination.

sentences: Metric k-means selects exactly k centers from an explicit candidate set.
Its objective is the sum of squared distances to the nearest selected center.
The card asks for the infimum of expected polynomial-time approximation ratios on arbitrary finite metrics.
The July 2026 preprint reports an upper bound approaching 4.9 without a matching determination.
The requested numerical precision is absolute error at most 0.01.
